findings.title: Do not curl|sh an unverified remote script in the build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads arbitrary content and executes it as root during `docker build` with no version pin, checksum, or signature check. `-L` follows redirects, so the executed payload is whatever the endpoint (or a compromised DNS/TLS-terminating middlebox) serves at build time. Any change or compromise of the remote script silently becomes part of the image, and the build output is non-reproducible because the fetched script is not pinned. This is an unreviewable arbitrary-code-execution path baked into the image.

findings.title: Do not curl|sh an unverified remote script in the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The added line `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes an arbitrary script fetched at build time as root inside the image, with no checksum/signature verification and no version pin. Whoever controls the URL (or the network path) controls the image contents; a build is a one-shot, non-reproducible artifact, so a compromise or a silently changed script ships to every consumer. It also swallows the download failure: in `sh -c 'curl ... | sh'` the pipeline's exit status is sh's, so if curl fails the build still succeeds with the install silently not performed. (TRIGGER D fires: the failure signal is mapped to sh's default success — see checked entry.)

findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script to shell at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: The only added line downloads `https://example.com/install.sh` and pipes it to `sh`, executing arbitrary remote content as root during the image build with no pinned version, no checksum/signature verification, no TLS pinning, and no `-f`. Whoever controls or can MITM that URL gets code execution inside the produced image, and the build is non-reproducible: the remote script can change silently at any time, so the same Dockerfile yields different bits. Because `curl -sL` omits `-f`, an HTTP 4xx/5xx that returns a body is piped into `sh` rather than failing the build, so failures are not even detected.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing with empty
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault discards the error from Load with `v, _ := Load(key, m)`. Load returns ErrMissing (@src/store.go:10) for an absent key, but also returns "", nil for a key that is present with an empty value (@src/store.go:12). Because the error is dropped, both cases now yield the identical result "". Any caller of this exported helper (there are none in-repo yet, but the exported signature is the public contract) is FORCED to treat 'failed/lookup-missing' as a real value, and acting on that fallback (e.g. writing, billing, or reporting the empty string as if it were stored data) is indistinguishable from a genuine empty value — the failure signal never reaches the decision point.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating failure with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing when the key is absent (src/store.go:9-11), and an empty string is a legitimate stored value in map[string]string. LoadOrDefault assigns the error to _ and returns v, so an absent key yields "" indistinguishable from a present-but-empty value. Any caller that uses this for persistence, defaults, authorization, or reporting is forced to treat a failed lookup as real data — this is an exported/public API contract defect present now, independent of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Run no longer waits for jobs; results delivered after return
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version sent `results <- j*2` synchronously in the loop, so Run returned only after every result was delivered. The change dispatches each send into a fire-and-forget goroutine and Run returns immediately, before any (or all) sends happen. Any caller relying on the old contract (the natural one for a `func Run(...)` that blocks until done) now observes a partial/no result set; if it follows the standard pattern of `close(results)` after Run returns and then drains, pending goroutines hit `results <- j*2` on a closed channel and panic with "send on closed channel". Goroutines also leak past Run (ctx is never observed, and there is no WaitGroup/errgroup join), so completion and cancellation are no longer possible.

findings.title: Run no longer waits for sends; callers see incomplete/panic behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run sent every j*2 synchronously and only returned after all sends completed. Now each iteration starts a goroutine (src/worker.go:7-9) and the loop returns immediately without a sync.WaitGroup or any join, so Run returns while sends are still outstanding. Any caller that reads a known count of results, or that does `close(results)` right after Run returns (a natural pattern for `chan<- int` where the producer closes), now either observes missing results or panics with 'send on closed channel' inside the spawned goroutines. The removed completion guarantee is the defect; it is present in the shipped function even though this repo currently has no in-repo callers to demonstrate it.

findings.title: Result ordering guarantee dropped by per-job goroutines
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation sent results strictly in jobs order (index i of results corresponded to jobs[i]). Round-tripping through independent goroutines removes any ordering guarantee, so a caller that pairs results positionally with the input jobs now receives values in nondeterministic order even once the completion bug is fixed. Because Run is an exported function whose observable output ordering changed, this is a public-contract regression regardless of today's in-repo callers.

findings.title: Run no longer waits for results; spawned goroutines outlive the call
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, Run sent every result inline, so returning from Run guaranteed all `results <- j*2` sends had completed (for an unbuffered channel, each send had been received). The new body spawns one goroutine per job with no WaitGroup/synchronization and returns immediately after the loop, so Run's postcondition is gone: a caller that does `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` (the natural pattern for a send-only channel it cannot close itself) now races the still-running goroutines and can panic with `send on closed channel`; a caller that reads exactly `len(jobs)` values and then proceeds can consume results while goroutines are still pending, leaking goroutines blocked forever on the unbuffered send. Concurrency is also unbounded (one goroutine per job, up to len(jobs) simultaneously blocked on the channel) and result order is now nondeterministic, whereas the old loop produced results in `jobs` order. This is an exported function whose whole observable contract was 'results are emitted synchronously'; that contract is broken.

findings.title: Log accepts `tag` but never uses it; tagging is a silent no-op
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature now promises a `tag` capability (a public, optional parameter whose only purpose is to annotate/classify the emitted log line), but the body `println(message)` at src/logger.go:4 discards `tag` entirely. Existing callers are unaffected, but any caller passing tags receives output identical to the untagged call and has no way to distinguish a dropped tag from a correctly-applied one. Because `Log` is exported, the signature itself is the contract; shipping a documented-by-name parameter that does nothing forces every caller to conflate 'tagged' with 'untagged' output.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord now grants cross-tenant admin and non-admin deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` (delete allowed only for an admin acting inside their own tenant) to `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. The disjunction is now true in two unauthorized cases: (1) any non-admin whose tenantId matches the record's tenantId now passes (previously rejected because isAdmin was false), letting ordinary users delete records they should not; and (2) any admin now passes regardless of tenantId, removing the tenant boundary and allowing admins to delete records belonging to other tenants. This is a public exported API whose contract is the authorization decision itself, so the defect ships now even though there are no in-repo callers.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord widened: non-admins and cross-tenant admins can delete
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate previously required session.isAdmin AND session.tenantId === record.tenantId; it now ORs them. Two concrete authorization bypasses result: (1) a non-admin user whose tenantId matches the record can delete records they do not own (ownerId is never consulted), and (2) an admin can delete records in ANY tenant, breaking tenant isolation. Both grant delete/data-loss access that the base revision denied.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord allows cross-tenant and non-admin deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` to `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. With OR, the delete guard now returns true in two previously-denied cases: (1) a non-admin session whose tenantId matches the record's tenantId, i.e. any ordinary tenant user can delete any record in their tenant (privilege escalation); (2) an admin session whose tenantId differs from the record's tenantId, i.e. an admin of one tenant can delete records belonging to other tenants (broken tenant isolation / cross-tenant data loss). Both are authorizations the prior `&&` explicitly rejected. There is no other guard in the file; this single boolean is the entire delete decision.

findings.title: clampPercent promises clamping but returns unclamped values
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename to `clampPercent` advertises a capped result in [0,100], but the body still computes Math.round((done / total) * 100) with no clamp. The one in-repo consumer `progressBar` trusts the promise: at src/progress.ts:7 it builds '#' .repeat(pct) and '-' .repeat(100 - pct); for any done > total, pct > 100, so 100 - pct is negative and String.prototype.repeat throws RangeError: Invalid count value. Any external caller of the now-public `clampPercent` also receives a value outside the range the name guarantees. The defect is newly introduced by the rename: the old name `toPercent` made no capping promise.

findings.title: Clamp clampPercent result or keep the old name
findings.whyItBreaks: The freshly renamed exported function clampPercent promises a capped percent (0..100), but its unchanged body returns Math.round((done/total)*100) unclamped: clampPercent(150,100)===150 and clampPercent(-10,100)===-10. Callers that now trust the name rely on a bound that is not enforced; the existing in-repo consumer progressBar (src/progress.ts:6) feeds pct into "-".repeat(100 - pct), so an over-100 pct yields a negative repeat count and a RangeError. Previously the neutral name toPercent made no such promise, so the rename itself introduces the mismatch.

findings.title: clampPercent name promises clamping the body does not perform
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed symbol NAME `clampPercent` promises its result is capped to [0,100], but the body is unchanged `Math.round((done / total) * 100)` (src/progress.ts:2) and clamps nothing. This is an exported/public carrier, so the name IS the contract. A caller trusting the name passes done>total (or negative/NaN) and receives an out-of-range value; the sole in-repo consumer `progressBar` feeds it straight into `"#".repeat(pct) + "-".repeat(100 - pct)` (src/progress.ts:7), which throws RangeError for pct<0 or pct>100 (negative repeat counts), so the misleading contract converts a should-be-clamped value into a crash instead of a clamped bar.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors and returns DEFAULTS, silently resetting user settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously parseSettings threw on malformed JSON or a wrong-typed field, so callers could distinguish 'invalid settings' from 'valid settings'. The new catch-all returns { ...DEFAULTS } for every failure, conflating a parse/validation failure with a legitimate default value. The only caller, updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20), takes that return value, sets fontSize, and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) at line 22. So when the stored raw string is corrupt (e.g. valid JSON with theme='dark' but a non-numeric fontSize, which used to throw 'bad fontSize'), the update now silently overwrites the persisted settings with theme:'light', destroying the user's theme instead of surfacing the error. Failure and the fallback value are indistinguishable to the caller, and the fallback is then persisted as if real.

findings.title: Don't swallow parse/validation failures into DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `catch { return { ...DEFAULTS }; }` (lines 14-16) swallows every failure the previous implementation propagated: `JSON.parse` errors and the `bad theme` / `bad fontSize` validation throws. The only in-repo consumer, `updateFontSize` (line 20), calls `parseSettings(raw)`, mutates `fontSize`, and then calls `save(...)` (line 22). Previously a corrupt or invalid `raw` made `updateFontSize` throw before saving, so the caller learned the settings were bad and the file was left untouched. Now `parseSettings` returns a legitimate-looking DEFAULTS object, `updateFontSize` cannot distinguish failure from real values, and it persists that fallback: e.g. `raw = '{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"x"}'` yields saved `{"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}`, silently resetting the user's `theme` and permanently overwriting the settings file. This is both lost data and a discarded error signal.

findings.title: Stop swallowing parseSettings errors; returning defaults silently resets user settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch-all converts every prior failure signal into a valid-looking default: JSON.parse SyntaxError (line 10), Error("bad theme") (line 11) and Error("bad fontSize") (line 12) no longer propagate. Callers can no longer distinguish 'failed to parse' from 'a real settings object equal to the defaults'. Concretely, updateFontSize (line 20) calls parseSettings on the stored raw settings; previously a corrupt/invalid record threw and aborted before the save, but now it returns {theme:"light",fontSize:14}, updateFontSize overwrites fontSize (line 21) and persists `{"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}` (line 22) — silently discarding the user's real theme and any other stored value (data loss) with no error surfaced anywhere.

findings.title: Report mixes builtFrom commit with artifacts from 'verified' ref
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport resolves commit = build.ref(branch) and reports it as builtFrom, but now fetches artifacts via build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")) instead of artifactsAt(commit). Because ref(name) resolves to an independent commit, the returned BuildReport exposes artifacts that belong to a different commit than the one it claims was built. Any consumer rendering this report shows the wrong artifact set for the reported build (stale/mismatched artifacts), a user-facing regression versus the base behavior which used artifactsAt(commit).

The branch argument no longer influences artifact selection: buildReport(build,"main") and buildReport(build,"release") return identical artifacts even though builtFrom differs. Callers receive a report whose builtFrom commit disagrees with the commit the artifacts were actually read from, so any consumer correlating builtFrom with its artifacts acts on the wrong commit.

findings.title: recentEntries no longer caps results to `limit`
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment still promises "Returns at most `limit` entries" but the body only reverses and, for limit>0, returns the whole array (`return sorted;`), dropping the former `.slice(0, limit)`. The only caller, renderFeed @src/feed.ts:9, passes 20 and builds `const out = new Array<string>(20)` then writes `out[i] = page[i]` for i < page.length (@src/feed.ts:10-11). findings.title: recentEntries ignores `limit`; returns full list instead of capped
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment and signature promise `Returns at most limit entries, newest first`, but the body now only special-cases `limit <= 0` and otherwise returns the entire reversed array. The `.slice(0, limit)` that enforced the cap was dropped, so any positive limit (e.g. 20) yields all entries. renderFeed calls recentEntries(all, 20) and copies `page.length` items into a 20-slot array, so once `all.length > 20` it grows past 20 and returns every entry — an unbounded feed instead of a 20-item page.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit; returns all entries instead of cap
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch replaced `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` with `const sorted = [...all].reverse(); ... return sorted;`, dropping the `slice(0, limit)`. For any `limit > 0` the function now returns the entire reversed array, violating its contract `/** Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first. */` (src/feed.ts:1). The only in-repo caller, `renderFeed`, calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` (src/feed.ts:9) and then copies into `new Array<string>(20)` with `for (let i = 0; i < page.length; i++) out[i] = page[i];` (src/feed.ts:10-11). Since `page.length` can now exceed 20, the loop writes out[20], out[21], … growing `out` past 20, so the feed is no longer capped at 20 entries. This is TRIGGER C contract drift: carrier promises `at most limit` (doc + parameter), body computes all entries (src/feed.ts:5), and renderFeed relies on the cap for its fixed 20-slot buffer.

findings.title: entry-count header includes stale entries excluded from rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds `const live = entries.filter((e) => !e.stale)` and renders rows from `live`, but line 22 still calls `headerLines(opts, entries.length)` with the unfiltered length. Before this change rows and count were both `entries`-derived and consistent; now `# entry-count: N` counts stale entries that are not emitted as rows, so any consumer parsing the header (sizing, iteration, integrity checks) sees a count larger than the number of tab-separated rows. Minimal case: entries [{path:'a',size:1,stale:false},{path:'b',size:2,stale:true}] → header says `entry-count: 2` but only one row `a	1` is emitted.

The serialized manifest header `# entry-count: N` therefore advertises more entries than the rows that follow, so any consumer that trusts `entry-count` to size or validate the row list (or to reconcile a manifest against a directory) sees a false count and a parse/size mismatch whenever at least one entry is stale. Previously count and rows were always equal.

findings.title: entry-count header disagrees with emitted rows after stale filtering

For any input containing stale entries the manifest now advertises `# entry-count: N` while emitting only N-minus-stale data rows, so a consumer that trusts the advertised count to size/verify the entry list (e.g. asserting row count == entry-count, or pre-allocating) gets a value that does not match the payload it just received. Before this change the two were always equal, so this is a regression in the output contract of a public exported function.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against pinned revision, not "latest"
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset contract (src/changeset.ts:7-8) states fromRevision is 'the revision the changed paths were computed against' and that consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision. The diff keeps fromRevision = store.resolve(pinnedTag) (line 17) but now reads changedPaths via store.readChangedPaths(latest) (line 18), where latest = store.resolve("latest"). The two fields therefore describe different revisions: consumers receive a changed-path list diffed against "latest" but are told it belongs to the pinned revision, so replaying/applying those paths on the pinned revision can drop, misapply, or fail on changes that do not exist between the pinned revision and latest. This silently corrupts the changeset's core payload.

The set of paths now describes a diff relative to "latest", a different revision than the one fromRevision advertises. Every consumer that replays changedPaths on top of fromRevision will apply a path set that does not correspond to that revision (missed or spurious files), silently producing an incorrect replay.
