findings.title: invalidate() now clears other tenants' cached value
findings.whyItBreaks: Because cacheKey ignores tenantId, invalidate('apiKey') deletes the single shared `settings:apiKey` entry that every tenant reads. A call intended to invalidate tenant A's setting silently evicts tenant B's cached value too, forcing spurious refetches and (combined with the key collision) making per-tenant invalidation impossible. The signature also dropped tenantId, so existing two-argument callers no longer compile.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey() now returns `settings:${name}`, omitting tenantId, while settingsFor() still calls store.fetch(tenantId, name). The Map is keyed per-name only, so the first tenant to fetch a given setting name populates the cache for every tenant. A later call settingsFor('tenantB','apiKey',store) returns the cached value produced for 'tenantA','apiKey' (cache.get(key) !== undefined short-circuits the fetch at line 14), serving one tenant's setting to another. Precondition substitution: name='apiKey' → cache.get('settings:apiKey') @src/settings.ts:14 → hit !== undefined branch → returns other tenant's value; store.fetch is never called. invalidate(name) at line 21 makes it worse: it can no longer evict a specific tenant's entry and no longer matches the previous key namespace.

findings.title: Concurrent reserve() calls oversell stock after adding await
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed code reads `remaining` at line 15, then awaits `this.store.save(...)` at line 17 before writing memory at line 18. The await yields the event loop, so two overlapping reserve(sku) calls both read the same `remaining`, both persist `remaining - 1`, and both set the map to `remaining - 1`. Two reservations are granted but stock drops by only 1 in both memory and store, overselling the SKU. Before this PR reserve() was fully synchronous (read + set in one tick), so no interleaving was possible; the newly introduced await is the regression. It also persists the same decremented value twice rather than a running total.

findings.title: reserve() await breaks check-then-decrement atomicity (oversell)
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() now awaits this.store.save() between reading `remaining` (line 15) and writing this.stock.set(sku, remaining - 1) (line 18). Two concurrent calls for the same sku both read the same `remaining`, both pass the `remaining <= 0` guard (line 16), both persist `remaining - 1`, and both return true — a single unit is reserved twice and persisted as the same absolute value (oversell/lost update). The base version was synchronous, so the read-modify-write could not interleave; inserting the await introduced interleaving that did not previously exist.

findings.title: Concurrent reserve() oversells stock: await between check and update
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() previously did a synchronous read-modify-write, which is atomic in JS. The diff inserts `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) between reading `this.stock` (line 15) and writing it (line 18). Await is a suspension point, so two overlapping calls for the same sku both read the same `remaining`, both pass the `remaining <= 0` check, both persist `remaining - 1`, and both then write `remaining - 1` into memory. Two successful reservations decrement stock by only one (both in the map and in the store), i.e. overselling. Example: remaining=1, two concurrent calls both return true with stock persisted as 0, so the last unit is sold twice.

findings.title: backoff unit swap breaks unchanged retry.ts caller (1000x sleep)
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff previously returned seconds, so callers multiplied by 1000 to get ms. This change makes backoff return milliseconds (capped at 30_000), and only src/net/poll.ts was updated to drop the *1000. src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still computes `backoff(a) * 1000`, so it now multiplies an ms value by 1000: attempt 0 waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min) and attempt>=5 waits 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 hours) between retries instead of the intended 1s..30s. The retry loop is effectively stalled, not merely slowed.

findings.title: backoff unit change leaves retry caller multiplying ms by 1000
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed from returning seconds (Math.min(30, 2**attempt)) to milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt*1000)). src/net/poll.ts was updated to drop its `* 1000`, but the other caller, src/jobs/retry.ts:12, still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. It now treats a millisecond value as seconds and multiplies again: attempt 0 waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min), and once capped it waits 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 h) per retry instead of the intended <=30 s. Retry loops effectively hang, a real workflow regression.

findings.title: retry.ts still scales backoff() by 1000 after unit change to ms
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (cap 30_000 ms = 30 s), and poll.ts was correctly updated to use it directly. But the other caller, src/jobs/retry.ts:12, was not updated and still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, i.e. it treats the value as seconds. Substituting the new value: at a=0 the sleep becomes 1000*1000 = 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of the intended 1 s; the cap makes it 30_000*1000 = 30,000,000 ms (~8.33 h) instead of the pre-PR 30 s. Retry delays are inflated 1000x, so a failing job effectively hangs for hours between attempts.

findings.title: Propagate the file Close error in Save
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version ended with `return f.Close()`, so a failure reported only by Close (e.g. a deferred write-back/metadata flush error) was returned to the caller. Head replaces that with `defer f.Close()` (line 13) and `return w.Flush()` (line 20), which discards Close's error entirely. A caller that checks the returned error can now observe nil (flush succeeded) even though the final close failed and the data may not be durably written — a silent data-loss path. Save is exported, so this is a public contract defect regardless of in-repo callers: every caller is forced to conflate a failed write with a successful save.

findings.title: Dropped f.Close() error on exported Save hides write failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code propagated the close error via `return f.Close()` (old line 20), giving the caller the final durability signal. The new code uses `defer f.Close()`, whose return value is discarded, and returns only `w.Flush()`. `w.Flush()` writes to the *os.File buffer via Write; the OS-level flush/close is where a deferred write error (e.g. ENOSPC/EDQUOT/EIO on NFS or a full filesystem) is actually reported. With the close error dropped, `Save` returns nil in that case, so every caller treats a half-written/undurable file as a successful save. This is a changed, exported/public path that discards an error signal (TRIGGER D); the API contract itself is now lossy regardless of whether an in-repo caller exists yet.

findings.title: Save drops os.File.Close error, hiding write failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the final `return f.Close()` (@base store/save.go:24) propagated any error reported when the OS flushes/closes the file; the only write-error signal after `w.Flush()` was this Close error. The change replaces it with `defer f.Close()` (store/save.go:13) and `return w.Flush()` (store/save.go:20), so a Close failure (e.g. delayed writeback, disk-full, NFS) is discarded and Save returns nil even though the data was not durably written. Callers can no longer distinguish a successful save from a lost write. The discarded signal is an *added/changed* behavior on an exported path (TRIGGER D), so no in-repo caller is needed for this to be a defect — the generic `error` contract is broken.

findings.title: page_window drops the last row of every page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: page_window builds its window from _window_bounds, whose docstring promises half-open [start, end) bounds (lib/pagination.py:18), but the loop iterates `range(start, end - 1)`, which excludes index end-1. The base version correctly iterated `range(start, end)` (4357cba:lib/pagination.py:19). Substituting rows=['a','b','c','d','e'], page_size=2: page 0 -> range(0,1) => ['a'] (should be ['a','b']); page 1 -> range(2,3) => ['c'] (should be ['c','d']); page 2 -> start=4, end=5 -> range(4,4) => [] (should be ['e']). So every page loses its final row and the last page is always empty. render_page (lib/pagination.py:40) and summarize (lib/pagination.py:52) both consume page_window, so all rendered output drops rows and the numbering gains gaps (page 1 starts at '3. c').

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) interval (docstring line 18; body `end = min(start + page_size, row_count)` lines 20-21), so `end` is already exclusive. The loop `for position in range(start, end - 1)` excludes the element at index `end - 1`, i.e. the page's last valid row. For rows=['a','b','c'], page_window(rows,0,3) returns ['a','b'] instead of ['a','b','c']; every page silently loses its final row. Base version used `range(start, end)`, so this is an introduced regression. render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) consume the truncated window, so displayed output is wrong.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page (range off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) where end = min(start+page_size, row_count) (lib/pagination.py:19-21). The loop uses range(start, end - 1), stopping at end-2, so the final row of each page is never appended. Base behavior was range(start, end) (base commit c8a4fe6), which included every row. Concretely page_window(['a','b','c'], 0, 3) returns ['a','b'] instead of ['a','b','c']; for row_count=5, page_size=3 page 0 returns rows 0-1 (drops row 2) and page 1 returns row 3 (drops row 4). render_page (line 40-43) and summarize (line 52) consume this window, so one row per page disappears from rendered output.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check returns expired entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: get() stored `storedAt` at set() time, so age is `Date.now() - entry.storedAt`. The original `< this.ttlMs` returned the value while it was still within TTL. Flipping to `> this.ttlMs` means the value is returned only once the entry is EXPIRED (> ttlMs), and a still-fresh entry (age < ttlMs) falls through to `this.entries.delete(key)` and returns null. Effect: the cache serves stale/expired data and discards valid fresh entries, inverting its entire reason to exist.

findings.title: pruneDone splices during forEach, skipping done jobs and mutating input
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element with `splice` while iterating with `forEach` shifts subsequent elements down, so the element now at the current index is skipped on the next step. With adjacent done jobs (e.g. `[done, done, active]`), only the first is removed and a done job remains in the result. Additionally the function now mutates the caller's array in place and returns the same reference, whereas the previous `filter` returned a new array — an observable side effect for any caller that still holds the original list.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check serves stale entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was changed from `< this.ttlMs` to `> this.ttlMs`, inverting TTL semantics. Substituting real values: entry stored 5s ago with ttlMs=10000 -> `5000 > 10000` is false, so the fresh entry is deleted and `get` returns null (spurious cache miss, evicts valid data). Entry stored 20s ago (expired) -> `20000 > 10000` is true, so the stale value is returned. Every read now returns the wrong freshness: expired data is served and live data is dropped.

findings.title: pruneDone splices during forEach, skipping done jobs in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Mutating the array with `splice` inside `forEach` shifts later elements into already-visited indices, so the element that lands on the current index is skipped. Substituting `[A(done), B(done), C(notDone)]`: index0 removes A -> `[B,C]`; forEach advances to index1 (=C, not done); B is never examined and remains, so the result is `[B(done), C]`. Consecutive done jobs are left in the output. The change also mutates and returns the caller's input array, whereas the previous `filter` returned a fresh array, so callers now observe destroyed input.

findings.title: TtlCache.get inverts TTL predicate, serves expired and drops fresh
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison was flipped from `< this.ttlMs` to `> this.ttlMs`. Now a fresh entry (age < ttl) fails the test, is deleted on line 21 and returns null, while an expired entry (age > ttl) passes and is returned as if still valid. This inverts the entire cache contract: expired data is served and valid data is evicted, so every caller sees stale values plus guaranteed misses.

findings.title: pruneDone splices during forEach, skips entries and mutates input
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing at `index` shifts later elements left, but `forEach` advances to the next index regardless, so the element immediately after a removed done job is never examined. With consecutive done jobs only every other one is removed (e.g. [done,done,x] returns [done,x]). It also mutates the caller's array in place, whereas the prior `filter` returned a copy, so callers that reuse `jobs` now see it silently truncated.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard in averageAmount (now returns NaN)
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` makes an empty input compute 0/0, which is NaN, not 0. The function is exported public API, so every caller that sums, averages, thresholds, or formats this result now receives NaN instead of a real zero; NaN silently propagates through arithmetic (NaN > x is false, formatting prints 'NaN') and is indistinguishable from a legitimate value.

findings.title: Restore copy in busiest to avoid mutating caller array
findings.whyItBreaks: `rows.sort(...)` sorts the caller's array in place; the previous `[...rows].sort(...)` sorted a copy. `busiest` promises only to return the busiest row, but now silently reorders the caller's input data, so any caller that still uses its array after the call observes a side effect it never opted into (e.g. downstream positional/paginated logic sees a different order).

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty input after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: The base guard `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` was deleted. For an empty array the reduce seed makes `total` 0, so `total / rows.length` becomes `0 / 0 === NaN`. Previously it returned 0. Any caller consuming this number (aggregates, display, comparisons) now silently receives NaN instead of a valid number.

findings.title: busiest mutates caller's array by sorting in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Base used `[...rows].sort(...)`, which sorted a copy. The new body calls `rows.sort(...)`, and Array.prototype.sort sorts the receiver in place and returns the same reference. This reorders the caller's array as a side effect, corrupting any caller that reuses `rows` (e.g. iteration/order-dependent logic) after calling busiest.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN on empty rows (was 0)
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`. With an empty array, `0 / 0` evaluates to `NaN`, so `averageAmount([])` now returns `NaN` instead of the previously guaranteed `0`. This is the common 'no data yet' input for an aggregate/stats helper; `NaN` silently poisons downstream arithmetic (any aggregate, sum, or comparison becomes `NaN`) and renders as "NaN" in UI or gets persisted, whereas the old contract returned a well-defined zero. Base line 7 (git show 108f89f:src/stats.ts) proves this is an introduced regression, not pre-existing behavior.

findings.title: busiest mutates caller's array via in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR replaced the defensive copy `const ranked = [...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)[0] ?? null`. `Array.prototype.sort` sorts in place, so `busiest` now reorders the caller's `rows` array as an unannounced side effect. Any caller that reuses `rows` after calling `busiest` (iterating in original order, paginating, rendering, or persisting) now observes silently reordered data. The returned value is unchanged, so nothing warns the caller that its input was reordered. Base line 13 (`[...rows].sort`) proves the defensive copy existed and was dropped by this diff.

findings.title: Fix lexicographic numeric sort in rankScores
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version computed the cutoff with a numeric comparator (`scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)`). The new `rankScores` calls `scores.sort()`, which converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically, then `reverse()`s them. For players [{2},{100},{9}] with n=2, ascending string sort yields ['100','2','9'], reverse yields ['9','2','100'], so the index-(n-1) cutoff is num('2') = 2 instead of the correct 9. The filter then admits score 2 and `slice(0, n)` returns [{2},{100}], dropping the legitimately top-2 score 9 and including a non-top-2 player. Any n-way leaderboard with scores whose string and numeric order differ (e.g. 9 vs 10, 100 vs 99) is mis-ranked.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores (default sort is lexicographic)
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically, so rankScores no longer orders scores numerically (the base code used `scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)`). The `cutoff` in topPlayers is read from this wrongly-ordered array. Substitution with real values: players scores [9, 8, 100, 50], n=2 → sort() gives [100, 50, 8, 9] (string order '100'<'50'<'8'<'9'), reverse() gives [9, 8, 50, 100], cutoff = scores[1] = 8, filter(score >= 8) keeps all four, slice(0,2) returns [9, 8] — the true top two are [100, 50]. Any leaderboard/formatBoard output built on topPlayers is correspondingly wrong whenever score magnitudes differ.

findings.title: Restore numeric sort in rankScores; default sort breaks cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator orders numbers by their UTF-16 string form, not numerically. The base code used scores.sort((a, b) => b - a). Here scores.sort() + scores.reverse() yields a lexicographic descending order, e.g. [10, 9, 100] becomes [9, 100, 10]. topPlayers then reads the cutoff as scores[Math.min(n, scores.length) - 1]; with n=2 this yields 100 instead of the true 2nd-largest 10, so players.filter(p => p.score >= cutoff) drops the score-10 player and returns only [{name:'c',score:100}] instead of two players. formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:20) renders that wrong result directly to users. Multi-digit scores vs single-digit scores (or differing digit counts) trigger the mismatch; correct behavior only coincidentally holds when all scores share a digit count.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() previously compared the computed HMAC to the attacker-supplied signature with hmac.compare_digest (constant time). The new `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature` uses Python string equality, which short-circuits at the first differing byte and leaks a per-byte timing signal. An attacker who can submit webhook requests and observe response latency can incrementally recover a valid signature byte-by-byte, forging authenticated payloads. handle() at app/webhook.py:14 uses this same return value as its sole authorization gate (`if not verify(...): return {"status": 401}`), so the weakened check is directly on the live authentication path. CWE-208 / CWE-347.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC compare in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() gates request authentication via handle() (line 14: `if not verify(...): return {"status": 401}`). The change swaps `hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature)` for the built-in `==`. Python's `==` on `str` short-circuits at the first differing character, so comparison time depends on the number of matching leading hex chars of the attacker-supplied `given_signature`. An attacker who can measure response latency can recover the expected signature byte-by-byte and forge a valid `given_signature`, bypassing the 401 gate and reaching `processor(payload)` (line 16). This is a security regression relative to the base SHA, which used the constant-time `hmac.compare_digest`.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() authenticates incoming webhooks: handle() returns 200 (and runs processor(payload)) only when verify() returns True, else 401. Replacing hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature) with the built-in `==` makes the comparison short-circuit on the first mismatching character, so comparison time depends on how many leading bytes of given_signature match the expected digest. An attacker who can measure response latency can recover the expected HMAC byte-by-byte and then forge a valid signature, causing handle() to accept an attacker-controlled payload and invoke processor() on it. This is the classic non-constant-time signature comparison defect; the previous base implementation deliberately used hmac.compare_digest. Additionally, `==` drops compare_digest's requirement that both operands be bytes/ASCII-only str, so the signature check silently accepts a widened set of input types.

findings.title: Balance updates escaped the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so a failure in any statement rolled back all of them. The refactor keeps only `_record_ledger` inside the transaction and calls `_apply_balances` on line 24 outside it. The two UPDATEs are now no longer atomic with the ledger row (nor with each other): if the debit succeeds and the credit raises, or the balances fail after the ledger commit, the ledger records a completed transfer while funds are not moved (or only half-moved), leaving accounts and ledger inconsistent. This is a lose/partial-apply money path.

findings.title: Balance updates commit outside the transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change all three statements (ledger insert + both balance UPDATEs) ran inside `with db.transaction():`, so they committed or rolled back together. Now only `_record_ledger` runs inside the transaction (line 23) and `_apply_balances` runs afterward, outside it (line 24). The ledger insert commits first; if either UPDATE in `_apply_balances` raises (e.g. second UPDATE fails, or the process dies between the two updates), the ledger already records the transfer while the account balances are unchanged or only half-applied. The ledger and balances permanently diverge, and `transfer` propagates the exception so the caller sees a failure even though a debit/credit may already be persisted. This is a partial-write/data-integrity regression on a financial path.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside a single `with db.transaction():` block, so they committed or rolled back together. The refactor wraps only `_record_ledger` in the transaction (line 22-23) and calls `_apply_balances` after the block exits (line 24), so the ledger row commits before the balance updates run. If `_apply_balances` raises or the process dies after line 23, the ledger records a transfer that never moved funds; if it dies between the two UPDATEs (lines 9-16), one balance is debited/credited without the other. The `_apply_balances` UPDATEs are also no longer rolled back with the ledger row, so the debit and credit themselves are not atomic. Concurrent readers can observe the committed ledger row before any balance change is visible.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, breaking timezone-independent day buckets
findings.whyItBreaks: The body changed from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate to getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. billingDay is an exported canonical day-string used for billing bucketing and, via sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8), for day comparison. The result is now a function of the runtime timezone rather than the instant: for the same Date, servers in different zones yield different 'YYYY-MM-DD' buckets, and the same instant that previously produced one key now produces another (e.g. 2026-01-01T20:00:00Z is '2026-01-01' under UTC but '2026-01-02' in Asia/Taipei). This silently reassigns events to the wrong billing day on upgrade and breaks idempotency/deduplication against any previously persisted UTC-derived keys.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time instead of UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line replaced getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. billingDay keys a billing period, so the result must be canonical across servers/hosts, but local-time extraction depends on the runtime TZ. For the same instant, e.g. new Date('2024-03-01T00:30:00Z'), the old code returns '2024-03-01' everywhere, while the new code returns '2024-02-29' under TZ=America/New_York (and other off-by-one values in other zones). Two services in different timezones, or a host whose TZ changes, now disagree on the billing day, misattributing charges/usage and shifting sameBillingDay dedupe boundaries.

findings.title: Restore UTC getters in billingDay to keep billing keys timezone-stable
findings.whyItBreaks: Base computed the day with getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a given instant mapped to one canonical billing day regardless of process/host timezone. Head uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate (local time), so the same instant now yields different strings depending on the runtime TZ (e.g. 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z is '2026-01-01' under TZ=UTC but '2025-12-31' under TZ=America/Los_Angeles). billingDay feeds sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8), so day-boundary comparisons, day bucketing, and any billing keyed off this string shift or split inconsistently across hosts/instances.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, leaking cross-tenant profiles
findings.whyItBreaks: The memo cache is process-global (src/profile.ts:7) and profiles are scoped by (tenant, account) — the fetched Profile carries both fields (src/profile.ts:1-5) and fetchProfile is called with the pair (src/profile.ts:17). Keying only on `account` (was `${tenant}:${account}`) means readProfile("tenantA","bob") returns the memoized Profile fetched for ("tenantB","bob"), including its tenant field, so a caller gets another tenant's identity/displayName and never invokes fetchProfile for the correct tenant.

findings.title: Cache key no longer scopes by tenant, leaking profiles across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: `key` changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account`, so the module-global `memo` is now keyed only by account. `readProfile('tenantA','acct',...)` stores the fetched profile under 'acct'; a later `readProfile('tenantB','acct',...)` hits `memo.get('acct')` and returns tenantA's Profile (including its `tenant` and `displayName`) without calling fetchProfile for tenantB. Two tenants sharing an account name collide, producing a cross-tenant data leak / wrong-profile result.

findings.title: Restore tenant in profile memo cache key to prevent cross-tenant collisions
findings.whyItBreaks: `readProfile(tenant, account, ...)` is keyed only by `account`, but the fetched `Profile` is scoped to `(tenant, account)`. Two tenants with the same account name (e.g. `acme:alice` then `globex:alice`) collide: the `memo.get('alice')` hit at src/profile.ts:15 returns the first tenant's cached Profile, so `globex` receives `acme`'s profile (wrong `tenant`/`displayName`) without calling `fetchProfile`. This is a cross-tenant data/identity leak and a wrong-value return on any shared account name.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error, returning "" on a public path
findings.whyItBreaks: The new try/catch converts the explicit `missing: ${key}` Error (and any other error) into the default value "", which is also a valid stored string. Callers can no longer distinguish an absent key from a present key whose value is the empty string, so failure silently becomes data instead of propagating to the caller as before.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch-all converts the deliberate `missing: ${key}` error into the same value that store.get(k) legitimately returns for a key whose stored value is "". Previously load() (and loadAll(), which maps load over keys) propagated the missing-key failure; now every caller receives "", forcing it to treat 'key absent' exactly like 'key present and empty'. Any caller that persists, routes, sizes, or reports on this value cannot detect the missing key and silently operates on the fallback. This is an exported/public path with no in-repo callers, so the unusable contract itself is the defect shipping now.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error, returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously load() threw `missing: <key>` for an absent key, so callers could distinguish a missing entry from a stored value. The new catch-all maps ANY failure to `""`, and since store is Map<string,string> a genuine empty-string value is legal, callers can no longer tell 'missing' from 'present but empty'. loadAll() (src/store.ts:12) inherits this: it now returns [] silently instead of propagating the error. This is an exported/public contract change that discards the failure signal for all future callers.

findings.title: Surface or log retryBackground failures instead of swallowing them
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported `retryBackground` catches every error and discards it (`catch { continue; }`, src/retry.ts:27-29), then returns `void` with no propagation, no callback, and no logging. After all attempts fail, callers cannot distinguish success from exhausted failure — the failure signal is silently lost, so a background operation that never completed looks identical to one that succeeded. This is a public API contract defect independent of any current caller.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows the final failure with no signal
findings.whyItBreaks: New exported `retryBackground` wraps every `fn()` in `catch { continue; }` and returns `void`. When all `config.retries` attempts fail (or `config.retries <= 0`, so the loop never runs), it returns normally with no error, no return value, and no callback. Callers cannot distinguish 'fn succeeded' from 'all retries exhausted', so any caller that logs/requeues/alerts on failure will silently treat a failed operation as completed. Because the function is a public export, the unusable contract ships regardless of in-repo callers. `retry` has the same swallow shape, but this PR introduces the new public path.

findings.title: Renamed/added required Config fields break existing retry() callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is an exported interface. The change removes `timeoutMs` and http://makes `retries` and `timeout` required. TypeScript consumers that previously called retry(fn, { maxAttempts, timeoutMs }) no longer compile (unknown `timeoutMs`, missing `retries`). Un-typed/JS consumers that still pass `timeoutMs` now get `config.timeout === undefined`, so at src/retry.ts:8 `deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN`; the guard `Date.now() > deadline` at src/retry.ts:10 is then always false (any comparison with NaN is false), silently disabling the timeout so the loop runs all maxAttempts with no deadline. The rename also drops the explicit millisecond unit that `timeoutMs` carried while the body still treats the value as milliseconds.

findings.title: Widened value type breaks: .length is invalid on number
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now `string | number` (line 2), advertising that numbers are supported, but line 6 computes `value.length` and line 7 renders it into `defaultValue`. For a number, `length` does not exist: TypeScript rejects `Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'` in the union `string | number` (compile/build failure), and at runtime `(123).length` evaluates to `undefined`, so the input would render "len=undefined" instead of reflecting the value. The widened contract is therefore unusable for the new numeric case and even changes the rendered output for existing string callers from the value to "len=<n>".

findings.title: Handle numeric value before reading value.length
findings.whyItBreaks: The interface now admits `string | number`, but the body unconditionally computes `value.length`. For a numeric value (e.g. 42) `value.length` is `undefined`, so `label` becomes `len=undefined` and the input's defaultValue is wrong. It also fails typecheck: `.length` does not exist on the `string | number` union (TS2339), so any `tsc`/build step breaks.

findings.title: Numeric `value` produces `len=undefined`: `.length` used on string|number
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff widens the public prop to `value: string | number` (line 2) and then computes `value.length` (line 6). For a string this yields the character count, but for a number JS has no `.length`, so `value.length` is `undefined` and the input's defaultValue becomes the literal string `len=undefined`. The type annotation promises numbers are supported, but the body implements no numeric branch, so a caller passing `12` silently gets a wrong label instead of the intended length. This is also a TypeScript error (TS2339: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'), so a typecheck would fail.

findings.title: Do not echo repository secret into deploy logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step assigns `secrets.TOKEN` to the env var `TOKEN` and prints it (`echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`). This writes the credential into the workflow's build log. Secret masking is only a best-effort exact-string redaction on the runner and is not a security boundary: it can fail when the value is embedded/transformed, is exposed via downloaded/archived logs, and the step provides no functional value to justify handling the secret at all. Any party with log access now holds a live credential that the prior workflow never touched.

findings.title: Do not echo the TOKEN secret into CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step injects secrets.TOKEN into the environment and then runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, emitting the credential to the workflow log. GitHub masks exact registered secret values in most cases, but masking is a best-effort display filter, not a guarantee: any transformation, partial printing, or masking edge case exposes the token to anyone with log access, and the pattern normalizes leaking secrets to logs and to any log-shipping/artifact consumer.

findings.title: Do not echo secret TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step puts `${{ secrets.TOKEN }}` into the step env and then prints it via `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`. This writes a live secret into the Actions run log. GitHub masking only redacts the exact secret substring and is a best-effort backstop, not a guarantee: any transformation (encoding, splitting, quoting, or a token not yet registered as a masked secret) loses the mask, and Actions logs are broadly readable by anyone with repo/org log access and are retained. Introducing a step whose sole effect is emitting a credential adds no function the job needs (it is not consumed by a subsequent step) and instead creates a secret-disclosure surface on every push.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer; default 1MB aborts large-diff reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` drops spawnSync to Node's 1MB default. `git diff <mergeBase> <headSha>` (line 140) and `git diff --name-only` (line 57) for any real PR >~1MB (lockfiles, generated/minified files, large refactors) exceed that; spawnSync then sets error.code=ENOBUFS and status=null, so the guard `res.status !== 0` (line 38) throws an opaque `git ... failed: ` (empty stderr), and runGithub marks the check as "review failed". These PRs were reviewable before.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer: large diffs now throw at 1 MiB
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer falls back to spawnSync's default of 1 MiB for combined stdout/stderr. git() is used to capture the full PR patch via git diff mergeBase headSha (line 140), which routinely exceeds 1 MiB on large PRs (lockfiles, generated code, snapshots). When the limit is exceeded Node kills the child, sets res.status to null and res.error to ENOBUFS, so the `res.status !== 0` check throws `git diff ... failed:` and the review aborts (the throw is before the try/catch at line ~172). Previously the 64 MiB buffer handled these diffs; this is a regression, not a truncation, and it breaks the workflow for large PRs.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer; removing it hard-fails large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. This git() helper produces the full PR patch via `git diff mergeBase headSha` (line 140), which routinely exceeds 1 MiB for large PRs. Verified on Node v24: a 2,000,000-byte stdout yields status=null, signal=SIGTERM, error=ENOBUFS with truncated output, so the `res.status !== 0` guard (line 38) throws `git ... failed`. The throw happens before runGithub's try/catch (line 176), so the whole review aborts with no check-run posted. With the previous 64 MiB buffer the same 2 MB run returned status=0 and the full patch. Note gh()/ghText() still keep the 64 MiB buffer (lines 19, 29), so the removal is asymmetric and looks accidental.

findings.title: Keep bundle.baseSha as the merge base, not the PR base tip
findings.whyItBreaks: `baseSha` (line 138) is `PR_BASE_SHA || merge-base(origin/main, HEAD)` — the PR base tip — while `mergeBase` (line 139) is `git merge-base baseSha headSha` — the fork point. bundle.baseSha previously carried mergeBase and is the diff base consumers use (the {{BASE}} ref substituted into the review/critic/deep prompts and the reported ReviewResult.baseSha); the project's invariant is explicit that bundle.baseSha is the merge base while the base tip is tracked separately (prBaseSha), and there is even a test fixture that advances the base tip so baseSha != mergeBase. Whenever the base branch advances after the PR branches, this now reports the base tip while the reviewed patch is mergeBase..headSha: the ref handed to the model no longer matches the diff range, so an on-demand `git diff {{BASE}} {{HEAD}}` (the critic prompt instructs reading hunks this way) would surface unrelated base-branch commits, and the emitted base ref is wrong.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox for codex exec (removed -s read-only)
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` launches `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 23-29) so the child agent runs shell commands against the repo under review. The previous args pinned `-s read-only`, a config-independent guarantee that the child cannot write files or execute mutating commands. After this change no `-s/--sandbox` (and no `--ignore-user-config`) is passed, so the effective sandbox comes from ambient configuration: `codex exec` sets `sandbox_mode` to None when the flag is absent (codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs:343-346), the legacy default is only read-only when no project trust entry applies, and a trusted/untrusted project resolves to the built-in workspace profile (codex-rs/core/src/config/permissions.rs:51-69). On this machine ~/.codex/config.toml additionally sets `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` and `approval_policy = "never"`, so the review subprocess now runs unsandboxed with no approval prompt. A prompt/diff containing attacker-controlled instructions (the normal input for this harness) can therefore execute arbitrary commands, modify or delete the repo under review, and exfiltrate local secrets/credentials — a regression from the tool's read-only-review invariant and a potential data-loss/security bypass.

findings.title: Dropping `-s read-only` lets review subprocess write to target repo
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 24) and previously forced `-s read-only`. With the flag removed, the sandbox mode is now omitted and derived from `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml`/project trust. In the codex CLI, an omitted `--sandbox` defers to `ConfigToml::derive_permission_profile`, which defaults a repo that has a trust entry (trusted OR untrusted) to `SandboxMode::WorkspaceWrite` (codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs:833-841), and honors any user-set `sandbox_mode`. Because `codex exec` is non-interactive (approvals never prompt), the model can then create/modify/delete files and run write-capable shell commands inside the repo under review instead of being confined to read-only — a sandbox bypass that can corrupt or inject into the code being reviewed.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox for codex exec subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: `-s read-only` was the only thing forcing the child `codex exec` agent into a read-only sandbox. Codex's baseline default is read-only, but `derive_permission_profile` (codex-rs/core/src/config/config_toml.rs) overrides the default to `SandboxMode::WorkspaceWrite` whenever the active project has a trust decision (trusted OR untrusted), and headless `exec` additionally forces `approval_policy = Never` (codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs). So for the normal case of a local repo the reviewer has trusted — including this repo, whose `~/.codex/config.toml` sets `trust_level = "trusted"` — the review agent runs with workspace write access and no approval prompt. Since Needlefish feeds attacker-controlled PR/diff content into that agent, a prompt-injected PR can now create, modify, or delete files in the repo under review instead of being blocked by the sandbox.

findings.title: Restore merge-base so PR patch/changedFiles stay PR-scoped
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR replaced `git merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` + `git diff mergeBase headSha` with `git diff baseSha HEAD` (and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)`). `baseSha` is `PR_BASE_SHA || merge-base(origin/main, HEAD)`, and `PR_BASE_SHA` is the base-branch tip, which is not necessarily an ancestor of the PR head. `git diff A B` is a two-dot tree diff: if the base branch has advanced past the fork point, base-only changes (e.g. a file edited on main after the PR branched) appear in the patch as reversions of content the PR never touched. Consequently `patch` fed to the reviewer and `changedFiles`/`changedPaths` (used by `inlineComments` at src/adapters/github.ts:58-64) are wrong: unrelated files are treated as changed and may receive inline comments, and the model reviews hunks that are not part of the PR. The removed merge-base was exactly the guard that produced the correct three-dot (PR-scoped) diff; the old form also diffed against `headSha` rather than the literal `HEAD`.

findings.title: Restore merge-base and PR_HEAD_SHA when computing PR diff
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the patch was `git diff merge-base(baseSha, headSha) headSha` and `changedFiles` came from the same merge-base, i.e. a three-dot PR diff. The new `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot tree diff: when `PR_BASE_SHA` is the base-branch tip and it is not an ancestor of the reviewed head (branch behind/diverged base — exactly what merge-base guards against), the diff pulls in base-branch commits as reverse changes. That wrong `patch` is fed to `review(bundle)` (line 166) and the polluted `changedFiles`/`changedPaths` (lines 140-141, 169) misclassify surfaces and can place/omit inline comments via `inlineComments` (line 63). Additionally, hardcoding the literal `"HEAD"` on line 139 silently ignores `PR_HEAD_SHA`: `headSha` (line 137) is still stored in the Bundle (line 165) and used as `commit_id`/`head_sha` for the posted review and check-run (lines 178-179), so the diff can be for a different commit than the revision the review is posted against, misaligning line numbers.

findings.title: Diff against base tip instead of merge-base pulls in unrelated base changes
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` normalization turned the PR diff into a two-dot `git diff baseSha HEAD` (and `changedFileSet` runs `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD`). `baseSha` is `process.env.PR_BASE_SHA` (the base-branch tip), which is only equal to the merge base while the branch point equals the base tip. Once the base branch advances, the two-dot form also reverses every base-only commit, so `patch` includes changes the PR never made and `changedFiles`/`changedPaths` list files the PR did not touch. The reviewer then evaluates a wrong patch, findings can be anchored to unchanged/PR-absent lines via `inlineComments` (which filters only on `changedPaths`), and surface classification is computed over polluted paths.

findings.title: Replacement-string $-patterns corrupt injected bundle/patch text
findings.whyItBreaks: `String.prototype.replace(searchString, replacementString)` applies special replacement patterns to a *string* replacement: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched placeholder (e.g. literal "{{PATCH}}"), `` $` ``→the entire template prefix before the match, and `$'`→the entire template suffix after the match (and `$n`/`$<name>` where groups exist). `bundle.patch` is raw diff text and `JSON.stringify(bundle)` embeds that patch, so any `$`, `$&`, `$'` sequence in the reviewed diff is rewritten instead of passed verbatim. The pre-change code wrapped each replacement in `() => ...` precisely to suppress this interpretation (verified at base SHA 79959e3, lines 25/32/33). Concrete failure: a diff containing `$'` splices the whole tail of critic.md/review.md into the patch/bundle slot, and a diff containing `$&` injects the literal placeholder token; the Codex candidate/critic then receives mangled or duplicated input and can produce a wrong review. Line 25 (`{{BUNDLE}}`) is affected identically via the embedded patch.

findings.title: Plain-string replace corrupts injected $ patterns in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a STRING replacement interprets special patterns: $$ -> $, $& -> the match, $` -> prefix, $' -> suffix. The base code deliberately passed a replacer function (() => JSON.stringify(...) / () => bundle.patch) so the inserted text was treated literally. Dropping the function means any injected content containing these sequences is mangled before it reaches the model. This is realistic here: bundle.patch (line 33) is an arbitrary git diff, and diffs commonly contain shell $$ (PID), bash $'...' quoting, JS regex-replacement $& in replace() calls, etc. Substituting, e.g. a patch line `echo $$` becomes `echo $`, and a JS `str.replace(re, '$&!')` becomes `str.replace(re, '{{PATCH}}!')` because $& expands to the matched `{{PATCH}}` sentinel. The same defect applies to the {{BUNDLE}} replacement on line 25 (JSON.stringify(bundle) includes bundle.patch). The review prompt is silently altered, so the model reviews content that differs from the actual diff — a correctness regression in the tool's core path.

findings.title: String replacers inject/mangle prompts via `$` pattern substitution
findings.whyItBreaks: With a function replacement the return value is inserted verbatim. With a string replacement, `String.prototype.replace` interprets `$$`, `$&`, `$\``, `$'`, `$n`, `$<name>` inside the replacement. `JSON.stringify(bundle, ...)` and `bundle.patch` (raw diff text of arbitrary reviewed code) routinely contain such sequences: regex replace strings (`$1`, `$&`), shell (`$$`, `$'`, `$\``), jQuery/template code. Example: a diff line containing `$'` makes `criticPrompt` splice in every character of critic.md after `{{PATCH}}`, and `$\`` splices in everything before it — the critic then reviews a corrupted/duplicated prompt and can produce a wrong verdict. `$&` replaces the placeholder with the literal `{{PATCH}}`/`{{BUNDLE}}` text. The base revision wrapped each value in `() => ...`, which is the only form that guarantees literal insertion.

findings.title: Restore commit_id in fallback review POST to pin verdict to reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary review POST still sends `commit_id: headSha` (line 89) and `postCheck` pins `head_sha: headSha` (line 184), but the error-recovery POST at lines 101-112 dropped `commit_id`. Per the GitHub 'Create a review' API, omitting commit_id defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. So whenever headSha is not the PR tip at fallback time (queued/stale run, or PR_HEAD_SHA pinned to a specific commit / git HEAD resolving to something other than the branch tip), a REQUEST_CHANGES/COMMENT verdict computed for one revision is silently attached to a different, unreviewed commit, while the check-run still points at headSha. The two paths of the same operation now produce semantically different reviews.

findings.title: Keep a signal for malformed findings instead of defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change normalizeFinding threw on any malformed finding, so the default normalizeReview(raw) (strict=true) rejected the whole review and normalizeReview(raw,false) dropped the bad finding. The PR removes every throw, removes the Number.isFinite guard, and collapses the strict branch (line 131 always maps). A malformed finding is now silently coerced: invalid severity -> "P1", unknown category -> "bug", missing file -> "", missing lineStart -> 0, and a non-numeric lineStart becomes NaN (Number("abc")). The failure signal is lost: a caller can no longer distinguish a malformed finding from a real one, and the review can emit/escalate a finding that cites no file and lineStart 0/NaN, violating the required contract that every finding cites a concrete changed file and positive line range. normalizeFinding is exported, so this unusable contract ships regardless of the (currently absent) in-repo caller.

findings.title: Stop coercing malformed findings to silent defaults in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: base normalizeFinding (git show 22c1462:src/shared/schema.ts:95-135) threw on non-object input, invalid severity, invalid category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and non-finite/non-positive lineStart/lineEnd; normalizeReview defaulted to strict=true (threw) and strict=false dropped malformed findings. The new body defaults every failure to a real-looking value: unknown severity -> "P1", unknown category -> "bug", file -> "" (previously trimmed and rejected when empty), lineStart -> 0 / lineEnd -> 0, and Number(non-numeric) -> NaN passes through unfiltered (no Number.isFinite check), while normalizeReview(raw) at line 131 now maps every finding through this coercion with nothing dropped. A caller receiving `{severity:"critical"}` or `{findings:[{}]}` can no longer distinguish malformed model output from a genuine finding: it now gets a P1/bug finding with file="" and lineStart=0, which can flip a verdict to changes_requested and violates the review invariant that every finding cites a concrete changed file and line range.

findings.title: Don't swallow malformed findings into fabricated defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D fired. Previously normalizeFinding threw on malformed input (invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd), and normalizeReview's default strict=true propagated that as a hard failure (strict=false dropped bad findings). The new body coerces every malformed field to a plausible value instead of surfacing the failure: unknown severity -> "P1" (line 98), unknown category -> "bug" (line 100), missing file -> "" (line 103), missing/invalid lineStart -> 0 or NaN (line 104), lineEnd -> 0/NaN (line 105), title -> "Untitled finding" (line 99); normalizeReview now always keeps them (line 131) and no longer accepts the `strict` flag (line 113). A caller parsing model output can no longer distinguish malformed findings from real ones — it receives an apparently-valid "P1/bug" finding with an empty file path and line 0/NaN that it will surface or post as a genuine review comment. The failure signal is both discarded and fabricated as real data.

findings.title: Restore repo selector on gh pr view for workflow_dispatch path
findings.whyItBreaks: These two lines run only in the `else` branch, which is reachable only on `workflow_dispatch` (on `pull_request`, EVENT_HEAD is always set so the `if` branch is taken). This 'Resolve PR refs' step is the FIRST step and runs BEFORE 'Checkout PR head' (line 42-46), so no repository is checked out and the workspace has no git remote. `gh` does not fall back to `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`; it shells out to git and aborts with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git` (reproduced locally: `cd /tmp && GITHUB_REPOSITORY=owner/repo GH_TOKEN=x gh pr view 1 --json headRefOid` fails this way). The command substitution then fails, no `head=`/`base=` is written to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the job fails/steps.refs.outputs.head stays empty, so the manual review trigger no longer works. The previous `-R "$REPO"` (with `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}`) explicitly removed this dependency on a checked-out remote.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo on gh pr view (runs before any checkout)
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (step at line 42), so no git remote/`.git` is guaranteed in $GITHUB_WORKSPACE. With `-R "$REPO"` removed (and no GH_REPO set), gh must infer the repository from a local git remote; in a non-git working directory it fails with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository`, which I reproduced against gh 2.98.0. gh does NOT read GITHUB_REPOSITORY (`gh help environment` lists only GH_REPO for repo selection), so this is the only resolution path. This branch is the workflow_dispatch/manual-trigger path (EVENT_HEAD is empty there; pull_request sets head.sha and never reaches line 38). Because the failure is inside `$(...)`, the gh exit status is discarded and `echo "head=..."` still succeeds, so the step passes with EMPTY `head`/`base` outputs; `Checkout PR head` then checks out the default ref (line 45) and the review step receives empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA (lines 56-57) — a silent wrong-ref review instead of an error. Previously `-R "$REPO"` made the step independent of workspace git state.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view in pre-checkout refs step
findings.whyItBreaks: This `Resolve PR refs` step runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (line 42), so on a fresh/cold self-hosted runner the workspace has no `.git`. Without `-R "$REPO"` (or GH_REPO), `gh` must infer the repo from git remotes and fails with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository`. Verified locally against gh 2.98.0: `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` is NOT honored, and only `-R <owner/repo>` / `GH_REPO` bypass the git requirement (both reach the HTTP layer instead of the git error). Because the failing `gh` call sits inside a command substitution in `echo "head=$(...)"`, bash `-e` does not abort (verified: `bash -e -c 'echo "h=$(false)"'; echo reached` prints reached, exit 0), so the step 'succeeds' with `head=`/`base=` empty, `actions/checkout` is given an empty `ref`, and the review runs against the wrong revision instead of erroring. Only the `workflow_dispatch` branch hits this (the pull_request branch uses EVENT_HEAD/EVENT_BASE).

findings.title: Parse candidate review strictly so malformed findings fail closed
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview's second argument is the strict flag (default true); strict=false maps each finding through normalizeFinding inside try/catch and silently filters out any entry that throws (invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd, or a blocking finding with confidence < 0.7). The guard on line 30 only re-checks summary and checked, which strict mode does not affect, so it never re-raises a dropped finding. A candidate response containing one real finding with a single malformed required field is reduced to an empty findings list, the critic pass at line 37-38 only prunes (never recreates) findings, and deriveVerdict then evaluates an empty list as 'pass' — a malformed-field parse error is downgraded into an approval instead of failing the run. The sibling critic parse at line 38 still uses the strict default, so behavior is also inconsistent across passes.

findings.title: Candidate pass silently drops malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Passing strict=false to normalizeReview makes it wrap normalizeFinding in try/catch and filter out (return null) any finding whose required field is malformed, instead of throwing. The candidate's findings feed the critic prompt built at line 34-36 ({{FINDINGS}} -> candidate), and the only findings returned are the critic's pruned.findings (line 43-48). So a genuine P1/P2 finding that carries one bad required field is silently removed before the critic ever sees it and can never appear in the result: the review reports no such finding (verdict can become pass) while a real defect was discarded. Failure and 'legitimately no finding' become indistinguishable. Note line 38 still calls normalizeReview(extractJson(rawPruned)) with the default strict=true, so the candidate and critic passes now validate inconsistently — the same malformed output fails loudly for the critic but is swallowed for the candidate.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed output as an empty clean review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes all five validation guards that threw on malformed review output (not-an-object, non-string summary, non-array findings/checked/residual_risks) and replaces them with `raw?.x` coercion to defaults. A truncated, non-object, or unparseable model response now returns `{ summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] }` — byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a valid review that legitimately found nothing and blocks nothing. Every caller (this is an exported public function; there are no in-repo callers, so the contract itself is the defect) is forced to conflate "review failed to parse" with "review passed with zero findings", so a broken/partial judge response can be reported and acted on as a clean pass. The former `throw` was the only error signal; callers can no longer detect the failure.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently discards malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change normalizeReview threw for non-object input, non-string summary, and missing/non-array findings/checked/residual_risks (see base lines 115-131). Now every one of those failure cases is coerced to a default: summary -> "", findings/checked/residual_risks -> []. The exported function returns a value that is byte-for-byte the same shape as a well-formed review containing no findings, so any caller can no longer distinguish 'the model produced unusable output' from 'the review passed with no findings'. Because normalizeReview is exported public API, every eventual caller is forced to conflate the failure with a real empty review — a failed run can be rendered/reported as a clean pass with no error surfaced or logged.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed review output as an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation threw (`malformed review output: not an object` / `summary missing or not a string` / `findings missing or not an array` / `checked missing or not an array` / `residual_risks missing or not an array`), so a caller could distinguish a failed/garbage model response from a legitimate clean review. The new body defaults every field: a non-object `raw` now yields `{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}` (lines 115-128). A caller that maps an empty review to a pass verdict (no findings, no residual_risks, empty summary) can no longer tell "model said nothing/clean" apart from "model output was unparseable," so malformed output is silently reported as a clean/passing review instead of surfacing a parse failure.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch loses PR ref resolution; reviews wrong ref
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow is still dispatched manually (`workflow_dispatch` with a `pr_number` input at line 10-14, allowed by the unchanged `if:` at line 24), but on a workflow_dispatch event `github.event.pull_request` is unset. The removed `Resolve PR refs` step previously fell back to `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid/baseRefOid/baseRef` in exactly this case; that fallback is gone. Now `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}` evaluates to `github.ref` (the dispatch branch/default branch), so the PR head is never checked out, and lines 45-46 pass empty `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` to `src/cli.ts` (line 35 likewise defaults base.ref to `main`, which may not be the PR's base). The manual review path no longer inspects the requested PR.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch path checks out wrong ref, passes empty SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch is still a first-class trigger (lines 10-14, required pr_number input) and the job if: explicitly allows it (line 24); --pr still reads github.event.inputs.pr_number (line 47). But a workflow_dispatch run has no pull_request payload, so github.event.pull_request.head.sha / base.sha / base.ref are all empty. The removed 'Resolve PR refs' step used `gh pr view` to resolve these for manual runs; the replacement silently substitutes: checkout ref falls back to github.ref (line 29) = the branch the workflow was dispatched from (usually main), not the PR head; BASE_REF falls back to 'main' (line 35); and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are exported as empty strings (lines 45-46). Manual review therefore checks out and reviews the wrong revision instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: This workflow supports manual runs: the job guard (review.yml:24) allows github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' and the required `pr_number` input (review.yml:12-14) is described as a manual trigger that reviews a given PR. For a workflow_dispatch event, github.event.pull_request is absent, so every pull_request-derived expression in the diff becomes empty: the checkout ref at review.yml:29 evaluates `'' || github.ref`, checking out the branch the workflow was dispatched on (normally the default branch) instead of the PR's head commit, and the env vars PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA (review.yml:45-46) are set to empty strings. The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step previously filled these via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid/baseRefOid/baseRef`. So a manual review now loads the wrong tree and feeds the CLI empty base/head SHAs, and BASE_REF silently falls back to 'main' (review.yml:35) even when the PR targets another branch — the manual path is broken.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer; deleting it caps diff output at 1MB
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1MB (1024*1024). The removed option raised git()'s stdout cap to 64MB. git() now feeds the entire `git diff base HEAD` output into bundle.patch (line 100), so any PR whose unified diff exceeds ~1MB (or whose stderr does) makes spawnSync abort with ENOBUFS: res.status becomes null and stderr is empty, so line 12's `res.status !== 0` throws `git diff ... failed: ` and the whole review aborts. Large diffs are exactly the change set a reviewer most needs, and the sibling gh() helper (line 33-36) still retains maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64, confirming the 64MB cap was intentional and load-bearing.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git(): dropping it breaks large-diff reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync now uses Node's default maxBuffer (1024*1024 = 1 MiB on Node v24; even smaller on older runtimes) instead of the prior 64 MiB. The git() helper is used at line 100 to capture the full `git diff <baseSha> HEAD` patch text. For any PR whose unified diff exceeds ~1 MiB, spawnSync aborts collection and returns a non-zero status/ENOBUFS error, so the guard at line 12 throws `git diff ... failed`, aborting runLocal and failing the entire review. The identical 64 MiB buffer is still present on gh() (line 36), confirming the removal is an unintended capacity downgrade rather than a deliberate policy.

findings.title: Removing maxBuffer breaks git diff for PRs over ~1MB
findings.whyItBreaks: git() now runs spawnSync without maxBuffer, so Node's default (~1MB) applies instead of the prior 64MB (1024*1024*64). The large-output call `git diff baseSha HEAD` (local.ts:100, captured into `patch`) and `git diff --name-only` (local.ts:101) can easily exceed 1MB on PRs touching lockfiles, vendored code, generated files, or large refactors. When the cap is exceeded spawnSync kills git and sets res.error.code='ENOBUFS' with res.status=null; the guard `res.status !== 0` (local.ts:12) then throws `git diff <sha> <sha> failed: ` with empty stderr, aborting the entire review before any output. The sibling gh() helper at local.ts:36 still sets the 64MB buffer, so this removal is inconsistent and reduces an intentional large-output allowance.

findings.title: Errored review downgraded from failing to blocking-neutral check
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block that handles a review failure now posts the check-run with conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure" (head line 191; base line 191 was "failure"). GitHub treats a check-run conclusion of neutral as passing for required status checks, so when the reviewer errors out the PR is no longer blocked from merging. This is also asymmetric with the success path: a completed review that finds problems still posts "failure" via VERDICT_CONCLUSION (line 52), so 'reviewer could not run' is now treated more leniently than 'reviewer ran and requested changes'. The user-facing summary text still asserts 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR.' (line 193), which contradicts the neutral conclusion.

findings.title: Don't downgrade failed review check from failure to neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub's error path posts the `Needlefish` check run with conclusion "neutral" (was "failure"). GitHub treats `neutral` as a passing conclusion for a required status check, and `VERDICT_CONCLUSION.needs_human` is also "neutral" (src/adapters/github.ts:44), so any external gate keyed on the `Needlefish` check can no longer distinguish 'the review itself errored' from the legitimate `needs_human` verdict and will let the PR proceed. The check's own summary still asserts 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR' (line 193), so the code now directly contradicts its stated contract. The only remaining failure signal is `process.exitCode = 1` on the enclosing Action step; if that step is continue-on-error or the required check is the check-run (not the workflow job), a PR whose review errored becomes mergeable.

findings.title: Error path posts passing check: failure->neutral fails open
findings.whyItBreaks: On any review error the catch block posts the "Needlefish" check run with conclusion "neutral" (line 191) while the summary still asserts "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR" (line 193). GitHub treats a check conclusion of neutral (like success/skipped) as passing for required status checks, so on repos that require the Needlefish check an errored/crashed review now merges through instead of blocking, whereas the pre-PR "failure" (base de35f72 github.ts:187) blocked it. Neutral is also the conclusion already used for the legitimate needs_human verdict (VERDICT_CONCLUSION line 53), so a crashed review and a completed-but-needs-human review become indistinguishable — the failure signal is downgraded to a non-blocking default.

findings.title: Restore trusted-tool isolation; PR head now runs its own review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow enforced the documented trusted-tool pattern: PR head was checked out to `target/`, the reviewer was separately checked out from the trusted `frankekn/needlefish@main`, installed, and run against the target, so a PR could not influence its own review and no PR code executed. The change deletes the trusted checkout and the two-path layout, then runs `corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 51) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts ...` (line 59) from the PR-head checkout itself. Consequences: (1) a PR author can edit `src/cli.ts` to emit no findings / a passing result, defeating the required needlefish check that gates merges; (2) any `postinstall`/build hook or `src/` code in the PR executes on the `self-hosted` runner (line 23) with `GH_TOKEN: secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` carrying `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` (lines 16-19, 56). The unchanged `if:` guard (line 24) limits `pull_request` runs to same-repo heads, so this is exploitable by anyone who can push a branch to this repo (i.e. write access) rather than fork contributors — still a real control bypass and untrusted-code-execution regression on a persistent runner. The new comment's justification ('this repo IS needlefish, so the PR checkout's own src/ is the tool') conflates dogfooding the PR's tool with reviewing it; reviewing a PR that changes needlefish is exactly when the trusted main checkout matters.

findings.title: Restore trusted-tool checkout; PR head now runs as the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The trusted-tool pattern was removed: previously the reviewer was checked out from frankekn/needlefish@main into `needlefish/` and installed there, while only the PR head went into `target/` (never installed). Now the single checkout is the PR head at the workspace root, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` runs against the PR's own package.json/lockfile (arbitrary lifecycle/install scripts on a `runs-on: self-hosted` runner), and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts --github` executes the PR's own `src/cli.ts` as the review tool. That step receives `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` under `permissions: pull-requests: write, checks: write`. A PR can therefore modify `src/cli.ts` to always emit a passing check (bypassing its own required review gate), exfiltrate the token, or run arbitrary commands on the persistent self-hosted runner. Because the workflow's own comment and the removed header comment document this exact isolation as the control that 'prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool', removing it is a deliberate regression of a security control, not a neutral refactor. (Exposure is limited to same-repo PRs by the `if` gate on line 24, but that gate already treats same-repo PRs as untrusted for tool modification, so the control was still load-bearing.)
