findings.title: Restore severity normalization; case variants now downgrade to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code normalized severity with String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() before matching SEVERITIES, and fell back to "P1". Head code does a raw, case-sensitive SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) and falls back to "P3". Any severity the model emits in non-canonical casing/whitespace (e.g. "p0", " p1 ") — exactly the inputs the removed normalization existed to absorb — no longer matches and is coerced to the least-severe "P3"; a missing/unparseable severity is likewise fail-open to "P3" instead of the previous fail-safe "P1". A genuine P0/P1 finding thus gets silently under-triaged (and can be dropped from the blocking set) rather than surfaced.

findings.title: normalizeFinding downgrades valid severities to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported normalizer previously coerced the incoming value with String(raw.severity ?? '').trim().toUpperCase() before the SEVERITIES.includes check and defaulted unrecognized/missing values to 'P1'. The new body does a strict SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity) and defaults to 'P3'. normalizeFinding is fed raw, untyped review output (normalizeReview takes `any` and maps over raw.findings at src/shared/schema.ts:132), so a legitimately serious finding emitted as 'p0'/'P1 ' (lowercase or whitespace-padded, the exact shapes the removed code normalized) now fails the strict includes check and is silently rewritten to 'P3'; a finding with no severity also collapses to the least-severe value. The old code preserved it as P0/P1. This misclassifies the review's own findings and, since severity is the merge-gating signal, can hide a real defect.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code computed `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and tested that against the uppercase-only `SEVERITIES` list, then fell back to "P1". The new code tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` on the raw value and falls back to "P3". Since `SEVERITIES` is `["P0","P1","P2","P3"]` (schema.ts:85), any severity that isn't exactly uppercase — e.g. `"p1"`, `" p0 "`, common in raw/LLM JSON — no longer matches, so it is silently reclassified to the lowest default. Concretely `normalizeFinding({ severity: "p1", ... })` returned `"P1"` before and now returns `"P3"`; a valid critical finding is downgraded two levels instead of preserved.

findings.title: Re-adding secret stripping removed leaks GitHub tokens to codex child
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted lines built `env` from `process.env` with GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN removed, then passed it as spawnSync's `env`. That option was removed too, so spawnSync now falls back to its default (`process.env`) and the spawned `codex exec` agent inherits every credential in the parent environment. codex exec runs an autonomous, prompt-driven model with repository and network access, so a poisoned prompt/repo can read these tokens from its own environment and exfiltrate them, and they can also leak into codex configs/logs. The comment-free removal of exactly those three secret names shows the sanitization was intentional, so this is a real secret-exposure regression rather than a cleanup.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code built `env = {...process.env}` and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, then passed that scrubbed `env` to `spawnSync`. The diff removes both the deletions and the `env` option. `spawnSync` with no `env` inherits `process.env` verbatim, so the codex child (which runs an LLM over repo/prompt content and is a prompt-injection surface) can now read GitHub credentials and exfiltrate them via its network calls. This is a concrete widening of secret exposure on the live execution path, not a stylistic change.

findings.title: Restore credential scrubbing removed from codex subprocess env
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the `const env = { ...process.env }` block that deleted GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and drops `env` from the spawnSync options. With no `env` passed, spawnSync inherits `process.env` verbatim, so the spawned `codex exec` process (and any command the model-driven agent runs inside it) now sees the GitHub credentials that were previously withheld. runCodex feeds untrusted content (raw PR diffs/repo text) into that subprocess, so an injected instruction can read process.env and exfiltrate the tokens — a credential-exposure regression in a deliberately-hardened path.

findings.title: Restore fork guard: untrusted PR code now executes on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted predicate `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only barrier keeping fork PRs out of this job. With it gone, the job runs for fork PRs and immediately checks out the fork head (`ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha`) and executes fork-controlled code on a persistent `self-hosted` runner: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` still runs fork-defined lifecycle scripts (postinstall/prepare in the fork's package.json), and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts ...` executes the fork's src/ directly. A malicious fork PR thus gains arbitrary code execution on the runner host, a classic self-hosted 'pwn request' (the `pull_request` event only downgrades GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only; it does not sandbox the runner host or stop code execution).

findings.title: Removing fork guard runs untrusted fork PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` restricted this job to PRs whose head repo == base repo. Without it, the job runs for fork PRs too, and the steps then execute code fully controlled by the (untrusted) fork author: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` runs lifecycle/postinstall scripts, and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` executes `src/cli.ts` from the PR head. On `runs-on: self-hosted` this is arbitrary code execution on persistent, usually more-privileged infrastructure (network reachability to internal services, retained caches/credentials), i.e. a 'pwn request'. The `pull_request` event does downgrade the token for forks, but that does not mitigate RCE on the self-hosted runner.

findings.title: Do not run self-hosted review on fork PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow gated the job with `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository`, which skips PRs originating from forks. This diff deletes that guard, so any external contributor who opens a PR from a fork now triggers this `pull_request` workflow on `runs-on: self-hosted`. The job checks out the fork's head SHA (line 23), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, executes dependency lifecycle scripts from fork-controlled manifests) and executes the fork's own `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` in scope. That is arbitrary attacker-controlled code execution on Frank's persistent self-hosted runner/host, the classic fork-on-self-hosted-runner compromise (the guard existed precisely to prevent this).

findings.title: Don't silently override explicit 0 runner timeout config
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0` makes readRunnerDurationMs reject a parsed value of exactly 0 and return fallbackMs. Substitute value "0": Number("0")=0, `0 > 0` is false, so the function returns the fallback. Applies to both callers: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 now yields 5000 instead of 0 (runner-process.ts:3-6) and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now yields 2000 instead of 0 (runner-process.ts:7-10). Those returns feed the SIGTERM grace and give-up setTimeout delays (runner-process.ts:123-124), so an operator who deliberately configured 0 to force immediate SIGKILL / immediate give-up now silently waits the default 5s/2s. The prior code explicitly supported 0 (`>= 0`); this is an unannounced removal of a supported config value with no error or log.

findings.title: Zero duration now silently replaced by fallback (over-block)
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs previously accepted an explicit 0 (`parsed >= 0`), so an operator could set NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 (escalate to SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM, line 117-118) or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 (stop waiting for `close` immediately after SIGKILL, line 119-123). 0 is a finite, valid millisecond duration and setTimeout(…, 0) is well-defined, so rejecting it is an over-block. The new `parsed > 0` makes 0 fail the predicate and return fallbackMs instead, so those explicit configs are silently discarded and the process-tree termination timing changes to 5000ms (line 5) / 2000ms (line 9) with no warning.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so no changed file is silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: The head keeps only the top-6 hotspots (`sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`, line 93) and the removed block added a synthetic 'tail-coverage' hotspot containing every `bundle.changedFiles` path not present in a selected hotspot, with the explicit contract comment 'never silently skip a changed file'. With that block gone, any changed file mapped to a hotspot beyond MAX_HOTSPOTS, or not mapped to any surface at all, is never sent to a deep pass, yet reviewLarge still returns a normal verdict and summary (lines 122-130) as if the whole PR were reviewed. On a large PR (>10 files / >30k patch chars) a file carrying a real defect can ship through a clean verdict.

findings.title: Preserve deep-pass residual risks into the critic candidate
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base, each successful deep pass contributed `res.residual_risks` into the `residuals` array that was passed to the critic as `candidateMerged.residual_risks`; the critic is the only producer of the final `residual_risks` used by `deriveVerdict` (line 122). Head hardcodes `residual_risks: []` and only consumes `res.findings`/`res.summary` (lines 103-105), so any `blocks:true` residual a deep pass reports ('could not verify X') is discarded and can no longer downgrade or block the final verdict — the review can return PASS while unresolved deep-pass gaps exist.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop: changed files are silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: The coverage backstop was removed. Previously, after `hotspots = sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`, every changed file not present in a selected hotspot was collected into a `tail-coverage` hotspot and deep-reviewed, so no changed file could be silently skipped. Now the loop at line 97 iterates only the mapped, top-6 (MAX_HOTSPOTS @line 26) hotspots; any changed file that the map pass did not assign to one of those hotspots — including files in hotspots dropped by the slice and files not mapped to any surface at all — is never deep-reviewed, and no `checked` entry or residual risk records the omission. The removed comment stated the exact invariant being violated: "never silently skip a changed file". The result is a review whose `checked`/summary can read as complete coverage while whole changed files were never examined.

findings.title: One hotspot failure now aborts the entire large review
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot try/catch was removed. Previously a failing deep pass (runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview throwing, e.g. a flaky model call or malformed JSON for one hotspot) was caught, recorded in `checked` as "DEEP PASS FAILED", and a `blocks:true` residual risk was added, then the loop continued so the other hotspots' findings still reached the critic. Now any error from the deep call at line 103 propagates out of `reviewLarge`, so `review()` throws and the caller receives no result at all: all findings and `checked` entries already produced for other hotspots are discarded, and the failure is not turned into a residual risk. This makes the large-PR path all-or-nothing on a single flaky sub-call.

findings.title: Restore the tail-coverage backstop so changed files are never skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted backstop computed covered/uncovered against `bundle.changedFiles` and pushed a `tail-coverage` hotspot for every changed file not assigned to a selected surface, explicitly so a changed file is 'never silently skip[ped]'. With it gone, `hotspots` is only the map pass's results after `sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (line 93). Any changed file the map pass did not map to a surface — or any file in a hotspot ranked below the top 6 and thus cut by the slice — is now never deep-reviewed, and nothing records the gap. A large review can therefore return a PASS verdict while changed files went unreviewed (false negative on the review gate).

findings.title: Restore deep-pass error handling; one failed hotspot aborts all findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The try/catch that wrapped each hotspot's `runCodex`/`extractJson`/`normalizeReview` call was removed (head line 103 now calls them bare). Previously a failed deep pass pushed a `blocks:true` residual and a 'DEEP PASS FAILED' checked entry and the loop continued, so the review still returned the other hotspots' findings with an explicit blocking signal. Now any transient failure (LLM call error, malformed JSON) for a single hotspot propagates out of reviewLarge, rejects review(), and discards the findings, checked notes and blocking residual from all other hotspots.

findings.title: Propagate deep-review residual risks instead of hardcoding empty []
findings.whyItBreaks: `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is now hardcoded to `[]` and the `residuals` accumulator was deleted. Each deep review can return its own `residual_risks` (including `blocks: true` entries that make deriveVerdict withhold a pass), and those were previously collected via `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` and fed into the critic prompt via `{{FINDINGS}}` (JSON.stringify(candidateMerged) at line 116). The critic no longer receives them, so unless it independently regenerates identical residuals they are dropped from the pipeline and a large review can report PASS while deep reviewers raised unresolved blocking risks.

findings.title: Don't drop bundle focus/deep from the large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge no longer forwards bundle.focus/bundle.deep into mapBundle (src/core/review.ts:83-89) and no longer substitutes {{FOCUS}} into the deep prompt (src/core/review.ts:117-120). focus is still a live, supported input: reviewSmall serializes the whole bundle via JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2) (src/core/review.ts:51-55), so focus still steers small PRs. After this change a user-specified focus is silently ignored on large PRs, and because prompts/deep.md is not touched by this diff its {{FOCUS}} placeholder is left unreplaced (the literal token leaks into the model prompt). deep is likewise dropped from the map bundle.

findings.title: Restore focus/deep propagation in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: Base reviewLarge built the deep prompt with `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` and put `focus`/`deep` into mapBundle. This diff deletes both, while `deep.md`/`map.md` are unchanged and the Bundle still carries `focus`/`deep` (reviewSmall still serializes the whole bundle at src/core/review.ts:52-55, so small PRs keep honoring focus). Result: identical user input is honored for small PRs but silently dropped for large PRs, and because the deep template is untouched the literal `{{FOCUS}}` placeholder (with no focus text) is now what the model receives. mapBundle (src/core/review.ts:83-89) likewise no longer tells the map pass the requested focus/deep.

findings.title: formatDuration can output 'Nm 60s' after independent second rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: seconds is rounded from the remainder independently of minutes. For any ms where (ms % 60000) >= 59500 the remainder rounds to 60, so when minutes > 0 the string becomes 'Nm 60s' (e.g. ms=119500 -> '1m 60s') and when minutes == 0 it becomes '60s' instead of '1m 0s' (e.g. ms=59500). The pre-change code rounded total seconds first, then split, so ms=119500 -> '2m 0s' and ms=59500 -> '1m 0s'. This value is rendered to users by renderMarkdown via formatDuration(s.durationMs) at src/shared/render.ts:75 and total at :80, so the malformed duration appears in the review output.

findings.title: formatDuration can render 'Xm 60s' when remainder rounds up
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code floors minutes from the raw value but independently rounds the sub-minute remainder to seconds, so when (ms % 60000) >= 59500 the seconds component rounds up to 60 and is not carried into minutes. For ms = 119500..119999 the function returns '1m 60s' instead of '2m 0s' (the old code returned '2m 0s' because it rounded total seconds first). This produces malformed duration text in the per-call and total lines of the rendered review report.

findings.title: formatDuration can emit '1m 60s' (seconds not carried into minutes)
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code floors minutes first, then rounds the remainder independently (Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000)), so the rounded seconds value can equal 60 instead of carrying into the minutes. For ms=119500: minutes=Math.floor(119500/60000)=1 and seconds=Math.round(59500/1000)=60, rendering '1m 60s' where the base version (round total seconds to 120, then %60) produced the correct '2m 0s'. The sub-minute branch is also affected: ms=59500 now yields '60s' instead of '1m 0s'. This is a regression introduced by this diff on a changed line.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0 contrary to its 'positive' contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `Number(value)` results of exactly 0 now pass, but the exported function name `parsePositiveInteger` and its message `${label} requires a positive integer` still promise a strictly positive value. This makes `parsePositiveInteger("0", ...)` return 0 instead of throwing, and also lets falsy/blank inputs through because `Number("")`, `Number(" ")`, and `Number("\t")` all coerce to 0, so an omitted/empty CLI or config value silently becomes 0 rather than being rejected.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0 despite promusing a positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was loosened from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `value = "0"` (or "0.0") now passes and returns 0 instead of throwing. The exported function name `parsePositiveInteger` and the unchanged message `${label} requires a positive integer` both promise a strictly positive result, and 0 is not positive. Any caller that relies on this parser to reject a zero/absent numeric option (e.g. a timeout or attempt count) will silently receive 0 rather than the previous validation error.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 despite promising a positive integer
